planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or spring in well-drained soil under high shade; California barberry occurs naturally beneath oaks and in mixed evergreen forest and resents heavy, waterlogged ground.

directions: Site beneath open tree canopy in well-drained soil, giving California barberry the dappled or filtered light of its native oak-woodland and mixed-forest understory from the California Coast Ranges and Sierra foothills. Its finely divided, glossy leaflets are more numerous and slender than those of the related Mahonia aquifolium, giving the shrub a lighter, lacier texture, and bright yellow flower clusters open in early to mid spring ahead of powder blue-black berries favored by birds. Once established it needs little supplemental water and tolerates the dry summer shade typical of California gardens, making it a useful evergreen structural shrub for a low-water woodland planting. Cut back older, leggy canes at ground level occasionally to keep the clump renewing itself.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or spring in average, well-drained soil; Undulata is a denser, more heat- and drought-tolerant selection than the species and is widely used for hedging in Europe.

directions: Grow in ordinary, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Undulata tolerates more direct sun and dry spells than most other Oregon grape selections once its roots are established. Its glossy, spiny-toothed leaflets are distinctively crimped and wavy along the margins, giving the foliage a rippled, more refined texture than the flat-leaved species, and it holds a good deep green through winter with less bronzing. Dense clusters of fragrant yellow flowers open in early to mid spring, followed by dusty blue-black berries. It suckers modestly to form a tight, uniform mass, which combined with its density has made it a popular choice for informal flowering hedges and mixed shrub borders; prune immediately after flowering to maintain shape.
sources: Hillier Manual of Trees and Shrubs

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in shade; this low suckering species from Sichuan, Yunnan, and Guizhou spreads gradually to form a broad colony rather than a single upright bush.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in shade to deep partial shade beneath trees, where Mahonia confusa spreads slowly by suckers into a low, broad, ground-covering colony rather than growing as a single upright shrub like most of its relatives. Its narrow, glossy, sparsely spined leaflets give it a softer, less prickly look than Mahonia aquifolium, making it easier to work around at the front of a bed. Slender racemes of small yellow flowers appear in late summer to autumn, an unusually late season for the genus, followed by blue-black berries. Once established it tolerates dry shade and root competition well and needs only occasional deep watering during prolonged drought; thin out old canes at the base periodically to keep the colony from becoming congested.

common_name: Golden Abundance Mahonia (Wagner's Hybrid Oregon Grape)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or spring in well-drained soil in partial shade; this Pacific Northwest hybrid selection is grown mainly for its unusually heavy flower display and colorful new growth.

directions: Grow in well-drained soil in partial shade, sheltered from harsh midday sun, which can bleach the foliage of this Mahonia aquifolium x Mahonia pinnata hybrid raised in Washington state. Golden Abundance lives up to its name with an exceptionally dense, heavy display of bright egg-yolk-yellow flower clusters in late winter to early spring, well beyond the bloom of an ordinary Oregon grape, followed by blue-black berries that draw birds. New spring foliage emerges with a bronze-red flush before settling to glossy dark green, adding a second season of color ahead of flowering. It is a tough, low-maintenance evergreen for a mixed shrub border or foundation planting; water during establishment and dry spells, and prune only to remove dead or crossing wood.
sources: Great Plant Picks — Elisabeth C. Miller Botanical Garden
